title: Can You Bring Food Through TSA?
summary: Learn which foods can go through TSA, which must follow the 3-1-1 rule, and how to pack frozen food, baby food, and holiday dishes.
body_markdown:
Yes, you can bring many foods through TSA in your carry-on. Solid foods—including sandwiches, baked goods, and cooked meats—are generally allowed. Liquids, gels, and spreads must follow TSA’s 3-1-1 rule: each container must hold 3.4 ounces (100 milliliters) or less, and all containers must fit in one quart-size, clear, resealable bag per passenger. Exceptions may apply to medically necessary items and food or drinks for infants and young children.


Here’s how to pack food for a smooth trip through airport security and onto your flight.
‍


## **The Basic TSA Rule for Food**


The simplest way to decide where food belongs is to consider its consistency.[TSA allows solid food](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/items/solid-foods) in carry-on and checked bags. Food that can spill, spread, spray, pump, or pour is treated as a liquid, gel, or aerosol.In a carry-on, these items must be in containers of 3.4 ounces or less and fit inside your one-quart liquids bag. Larger amounts should go in checked baggage when permitted.


All items are subject to screening, and the TSA officer at the checkpoint makes the final decision. Your airline’s baggage policies and your destination’s customs requirements may also impose additional restrictions.
‍


## **Which Foods Can You Bring in a Carry-On?**


The following table summarizes the general rules. If you’re unsure how to classify a food, check TSA’s guidance for that specific item before packing.


Food Type Carry-On Guidance Checked-Bag Guidance


Sandwiches, bread, cookies, cakes, and other solid foods Generally allowed Allowed


Cooked meat, hard cheese, and solid casseroles Generally allowed Allowed


Yogurt, hummus, nut butter, jam, salsa, and other spreads Containers must be 3.4 ounces or less Allowed


Soup, gravy, syrup, salad dressing, and other liquids Containers must be 3.4 ounces or less Allowed


Frozen food with ice packs Allowed when cooling packs are frozen solid at screening Allowed, subject to airline baggage rules


Baby food, formula, breast milk, and toddler drinks Special exception; larger quantities are allowed with additional screening Allowed


Canned food May require additional screening; TSA recommends checking or shipping some cans Allowed


‍


## **Solid Foods Are Generally Allowed**


Most everyday travel snacks and meals can go in your carry-on, including sandwiches, pizza, granola bars, crackers, candy, dry cereal, cookies, bread, and firm fruit.


Homemade meals may also be allowed if they are solid. Cooked meat, solid pasta dishes, and casseroles without loose liquid are generally permitted Pack food in a secure container that will not leak or open inside your bag.


TSA may ask you to separate food from your carry-on because dense or cluttered items can make the X-ray image harder to read. Keep food somewhere accessible so you can take it out without unpacking the entire bag.
‍


## **Liquid and Spreadable Foods Must Follow the 3-1-1 Rule**


The 3-1-1 rule applies to foods that are liquid, creamy, gel-like, or spreadable. This includes yogurt, hummus, nut butter, dips, jams, jellies, sauces, soups, stews, gravy, and salad dressing.


Each container in your carry-on must hold no more than 3.4 ounces, or 100 milliliters. All liquids, gels, and aerosols must fit in one quart-size bag. A larger jar or container is not allowed simply because it contains a smaller amount.


To bring more than 3.4 ounces, pack the container in checked baggage when permitted.
‍


## **Can You Bring Thanksgiving and Holiday Food Through TSA?**


Many holiday dishes can travel in a carry-on when they are solid. TSA allows pies, cakes, cookies, turkey, ham, stuffing, and solid casseroles through the checkpoint. Cooked macaroni and cheese can also travel when it is packed as a solid dish.


Gravy, cranberry sauce, preserves, maple syrup, and other foods that can be poured or spread must follow the 3.4-ounce carry-on limit. Larger containers can be packed in checked baggage.


The consistency of the food matters more than the type of dish. A firm casserole may be allowed in a carry-on, while a similar food with loose sauce may be subject to the liquids rule. If you’re unsure, review[TSA’s food guidance](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/food) before packing.
‍


## **Can You Bring Frozen Food and Ice Packs Through TSA?**


You can bring frozen meat, seafood, and other solid food in a carry-on or checked bag. If you use ice or ice packs, they must be frozen solid when you reach airport security. If they are partially melted and liquid has collected in the container, they may not be allowed through the checkpoint.


The rules are different for cooling accessories used with formula, breast milk, toddler drinks, and baby food. These packs can receive additional screening even when partially frozen or slushy.


Dry ice is another option, but it comes with stricter requirements. The FAA limits travelers to 5.5 pounds of properly vented and marked dry ice, and the airline must approve it. Confirm the airline’s policy before packing.
‍


## **Baby Food, Formula and Breast Milk Have Special Rules**


Formula, breast milk, toddler drinks, and baby or toddler food can exceed 3.4 ounces in a carry-on. They do not need to fit inside the quart-sized liquids bag and are treated as medically necessary liquids.


Tell the TSA officer about these items at the start of screening and remove them from your bag for separate inspection. Your child does not need to be traveling with you to bring breast milk, formula, and related cooling supplies.


TSA recommends clear or translucent bottles when possible because they can be easier to screen. Review the agency’s current[guidance for traveling with children](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/tsa-cares/traveling-children) before your trip.
‍


## **International Flights Have Additional Food Rules**


Passing through TSA does not guarantee that you can take the food into another country. Your destination may restrict meat, dairy, fruit, vegetables, seeds, and other agricultural products.


The same applies when you return to the United States.[U.S. Customs and Border Protection](https://www.cbp.gov/travel/international-visitors/agricultural-items) requires travelers to declare agricultural items, including meats, fruits, vegetables and products made from plants or animals. Items may be inspected, restricted, or prohibited based on their origin.


Check your destination’s customs rules before packing. Keep original packaging and receipts when available, and declare food when required.
‍


## **Keep Perishable Food Safe While Traveling**


TSA rules determine whether an item can pass through airport security. They do not determine whether the food will remain safe to eat.


The FDA recommends keeping cold food at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below. Perishable food should not remain at room temperature for more than two hours, or one hour when the temperature is above 90 degrees. Use a well-insulated cooler with frozen ice packs and consider the full trip—including airport time, flight time, and transportation after landing.


If you cannot keep the food at a safe temperature, ship it with appropriate cooling or buy it at your destination instead.
‍


## **How to Pack Food for Airport Security**


Choose containers that close securely and prevent leaks. Pack food in an easy-to-reach part of your carry-on in case TSA asks you to remove it for separate screening.


Separate liquids and spreads into containers that meet the 3.4-ounce limit. Check ice packs before leaving for the airport to make sure they are frozen solid.


Do not rely on appearance or labeling to guarantee that an item will pass. Search the TSA “What Can I Bring?” tool or contact AskTSA if you have questions about a specific food.
‍
